flashcards.q: Why does a.__add__ = custom_func on an instance not change what a+b computes?
flashcards.a: Operators dispatch via type(a).__add__, never via instance __dict__ -- the interpreter never consults the instance for dunder-triggered protocol behavior, only the type. Ordinary a.method() calls DO check the instance first; this rule is specific to implicitly-invoked dunders.

flashcards.q: Descriptor precedence order for obj.attr when attr is defined on the class?
flashcards.a: Data descriptor (__get__+__set__/__delete__) > instance __dict__ > non-data descriptor (__get__ only) > plain class attribute.

flashcards.q: Why does obj.name = 'x' raise AttributeError for a read-only property instead of creating an instance attribute?
flashcards.a: property is a DATA descriptor even without an explicit setter -- its default __set__ raises AttributeError. Data descriptors always outrank instance __dict__ for assignment, so the write never falls through to obj.__dict__.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between what a metaclass's __new__/__init__ controls vs a regular class's?
flashcards.a: A regular class's __new__/__init__ control INSTANCE creation (runs every call). A metaclass's __new__/__init__ control CLASS creation itself -- runs once, when the 'class Foo:' statement executes, before any instance exists.

flashcards.q: Why prefer __init_subclass__ over a custom metaclass for 'run logic when a subclass is defined'?
flashcards.a: __init_subclass__ (PEP 487) covers this exact use case without introducing metaclass-conflict risk (TypeError when combining base classes with unrelated, non-subclassing metaclasses) -- reserve metaclasses for needing to modify the namespace dict BEFORE the class object is built.

flashcards.q: Why is naive depth-first-left-to-right MRO wrong for diamond inheritance D(B,C) where both inherit A?
flashcards.a: DFS gives [D,B,A,C,A,object], letting A's methods resolve before C is even consulted, violating local precedence order (D listed B before C). C3 linearization gives [D,B,C,A,object] instead, guaranteeing local precedence order and monotonicity.

flashcards.q: Why does overriding __eq__ without __hash__ make a class unhashable?
flashcards.a: Python requires equal objects to hash equal for dict/set correctness. The inherited default identity-based __hash__ would likely violate this once __eq__ changes, so Python defensively sets __hash__=None automatically whenever __eq__ is overridden without an explicit __hash__.

flashcards.q: Why must functools.cached_property be a NON-data descriptor (no __set__) to cache efficiently?
flashcards.a: Non-data descriptors rank below instance __dict__. After first access computes and stores the value in instance.__dict__, later lookups find it there and skip __get__ entirely. A data descriptor (with __set__) would always intercept, requiring an explicit cache-check on every access.

flashcards.q: What causes 'TypeError: metaclass conflict' and how do you fix it?
flashcards.a: Two base classes have unrelated metaclasses (neither a subclass of the other), so Python can't determine a consistent metaclass for the combined subclass. Fix: define a combined metaclass inheriting from both conflicting metaclasses and pass it explicitly.

flashcards.q: Does CPython 3.11+'s specializing adaptive interpreter change data-model semantics?
flashcards.a: No -- it caches/specializes bytecode for observed types at a call site purely as an internal execution speedup, transparently de-specializing if a different type appears. The data model's observable semantics are unchanged; only execution speed differs.
